beats.text: A plant extract kills Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite behind Chagas disease.
But an extract is a mixture of hundreds of compounds. So which one did it?
Isolating a single molecule costs weeks of chromatography. Guess wrong, and those weeks are gone.
The obvious shortcut doesn't work. Across sixteen hundred ENPKG extracts, rotenoid content barely tracks activity: a Spearman rho of 0.095.
The most rotenoid-rich extract in the whole library is not even a selective active.
And candidates travel together. 486 rotenoid pairs co-occur in at least three extracts, so each compound gives the other an alibi.
In pooled screening, you design the pools. Here, nature composed them. Our only freedom is which extract to assay next.
DECOUPLE turns that freedom into a decision, under a strict budget of three assays.
First, attribution is continuous in log-abundance. Extracts that separate two compounds often carry one of them only at trace level, so simple presence or absence says very little.
Below a detection floor, a sample is treated as uninformative, not as negative.
Second, four explanations compete: compound A alone, B alone, both together, or neither. Every assay updates their probabilities.
Third, adaptive contrast scores each unassayed extract by how far it would pull apart the explanations the evidence can't yet separate.
It recomputes after every pick, with a penalty for redundant extracts. The goal is to find the extract where the suspects come apart.
Here it is on measured ENPKG data: a methyl xanthone, and a rotenoid.
Two starting hits carry only the rotenoid. But a third, jicama leaves, is active with just a trace of the xanthone.
So the rotenoid alone holds 39.7 percent, and both together hold 60.3.
Adaptive contrast picks an Uncarina decaryi extract with about thirty-five times more xanthone, and no detected rotenoid.
If the xanthone mattered, this extract should respond. It comes back inactive.
The joint explanation collapses, and rotenoid alone jumps to 99.9 percent.
Two confirming assays later, DECOUPLE nominates the rotenoid, and its second readout says it is not the host-toxicity driver.
On the same budget, the strongest-first rule ends with a two-way shortlist.
Our headline is about what gets nominated. Potency alone is a trap.
Rotenone is the most potent rotenoid, and the worst candidate. Its selectivity index is 51.7, against more than eleven hundred for deguelin and nineteen hundred for tephrosin.
In the real screen, 7 of the 15 extracts with over 80 percent inhibition of Trypanosoma cruzi are also toxic to host cells.
ENPKG measures host-cell toxicity on the same extracts, in the same screen. So every reveal buys both readouts, at no extra assay cost.
On semi-synthetic benchmarks, selectivity-aware nomination keeps developable accuracy identical, at 32.7 percent,
while wasted isolations fall from 32 per hundred episodes to 0.21. That is 154 times fewer.
Those rates depend on an assumed cytotoxic prevalence of fifty percent. The result is supported in simulation. It is not validated.
We benchmarked on 952 semi-synthetic episodes from 238 real compound pairs. The abundances and co-occurrence are real; the response is simulated.
On the hard stratum, sixteen pairs, spending no assays nominates correctly 8.6 percent of the time. Three random extracts: the same.
Three well-chosen extracts roughly double that, to 19 percent.
But adaptive contrast ties the chemist's strongest-first rule, with a margin of exactly zero. We do not claim to beat current practice. The value is in what it nominates.
In this benchmark, every nomination it made was correct. And on the full real library, it abstains, which is the right answer when the signal is that weak.
The rotenoid finding itself belongs to Gaudry and colleagues. We reproduce it as a pipeline check, not as our discovery.
The chemistry lines up with traditional knowledge. Jicama's root is eaten as food, while its seeds and leaves are used as insecticide and fish poison.
In the screen, that split appears as a gradient inside one plant: leaves, 65 percent rotenoid share and full inhibition. Woody stems, 12 percent and about half. Roots, 4 percent and none.
Three of six active species carry relevant traditional use, including Melochia umbellata, a Cameroonian antimalarial with no rotenoids at all. We treat it as a lead, not an identification.
We rejected a traditional-use claim we could not substantiate, and we claim no ownership of the knowledge described.
Occurrence is not abundance. Association is not causation.
DECOUPLE chooses the assays that pull candidates apart, says both or neither when that is the honest answer, and vetoes cytotoxic decoys before a chemist spends weeks at the bench.
Thank you.
